utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination is continuing, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Witness K. I should like to get a clarification of one thing that you mentioned, namely, that at that round table, the programme broadcast over Radio Samac, a citizen nicknamed Ibela took part; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that Ibela is in fact Ibrahim Salkic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that Mr Ibrahim Salkic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some sort of interference. I can't hear Mr. Boro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we check the equipment? Maybe the volume or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the same problem as before, Your Honours. We can now switch to channel 6, but if we have to use the interpretation, then we'll have a problem. Yesterday, we were able to see the witness and the interpretation on the same channel, which is not the case today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I was just informed by the technical people that they have to put their channel on channel 7. If they put it on channel 7, they are supposed to hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we try? Can counsel ask an innocent question for testing purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. K, would you be so kind as to count to 5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is the witness able to hear counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the counsel would say something, I could check.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. K, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. And the other parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it appears that our clients are receiving the English translation on the channel 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And yesterday it was channel 6 for B/C/S? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: First of all, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear you very well. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it's all right now. All right. The cross-examination can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that Mr. Ibrahim Salkic was a member of the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, since I didn't belong to it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We've discussed yesterday your meeting with Mr. Zaric. Can we agree that on that occasion Mr. Zaric said to you that he was going to do whatever is in his power to help you and your family somehow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that in my testimony. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, Zaric didn't ask you whether you belonged to any political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knew. He couldn't ask me. I really don't remember, sir, whether he specifically asked me whether I belonged to a party or not. He knew it very well, because I had told him then to leave me, my family, and my property alone, that I didn't belong to any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that on that occasion Mr. Zaric did not ask you whether your husband was a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't, but I asked him why he did not include my son in the 4th Detachment. He told me, "Because you have only one." And I told him that that's not true. He didn't do that because my husband was a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that on that occasion Mr. Zaric did not ask you why your husband and your son had not responded to the mobilisation call-up proclaimed by the Presidency of the SFRY on the 31st of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. My husband did respond, and he got a war assignment in Derventa. He -- he didn't ask me, and my son did respond.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It's not the husband; it's the son.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son did respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have some break between question, answer, question? While she is giving -- while we are hearing her answer, he's asking the second question and we have no opportunity to object if there's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel and the witness, please do pause and allow the interpreters to complete. In most cases -- I think in all languages, it's one person who interprets the answer -- the question and then the answer, so you have to pause to allow for the complete -- the completion of the work of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, another -- I'm sorry. Another thing is that the transcript doesn't say -- it says here, on page 4, line 4, "That's not true. My husband did respond." And actually, the witness said, "My son did respond."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. If you look -- yes. The interpreter corrected that. It's not the husband; it's the son.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Part of the problem is the overlapping, I think. Yes, you can proceed, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that Simo Zaric did not differentiate between people according to their ethnic, religious, or other background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, I could agree that was true, but during the war, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you attended the founding assembly of the SDA as a guest of honour in Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When you refer to a statement, counsel, please always direct us to which statement, whether it was the one obtained before the trial or whether it's the testimony in Court. You should be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall clarify that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You testified to that before this Court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. If you asked me, I probably answered. I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the SDA was a national and religious party of the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, just as the SDS and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This fact that it was a national and religious party of the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was that the reason why you did not become a member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to join a party, any sort of party, but my town of Bosanski Samac, probably because I was so capable, never gave me the opportunity to become a member of the then ruling party, the Communist Party, so I tried to join a mononational party later, since I couldn't enter the Communist Party. But I found out that I had no sympathy for either of the three of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam President. I believe that the witness said, "I hate them all." That was the last part of her answer. For the clarification, maybe my colleague can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. There is also one are issue. Page 5, line 13. It is obvious that this is not the answer. It says, "He why" or something like that, and we heard "yes" as an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we just have the question asked again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, I think on the line 13, rather strange he/why statement, you then did pose the question again and the witness did answer. You said, on line 20, "You testified to that before this Court; is that correct?" The witness answered, "I can't remember. If you asked me, I probably answered. I said yes." So that's clarified. It's only the other issue that was raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the next question, the one Mr. Pantelic was pointing out that the -- the last part of the answer was not -- is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said, and it wasn't recorded, what kind of attitude you had towards national parties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't accept them, because I come from a family which is mixed to such an extent that we don't know what kind of mixture it is, so we cannot stomach national parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you please confirm that a minute ago you said you hated them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all they brought upon us, I do hate them, I mean the national parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Your husband was issued with a weapon on the 16th of April, 1992 in the building of the command of the Territorial Defence in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had the opportunity to ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I've told you already, you could have asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that your husband was on the list of self-organised citizens of the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that such a list existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: That list was drawn up during the war, and it was because of such lists that were published in the bulletin of the Serbian Samac, we got into a lot of trouble, because if something is on the list and is not supported by a formal decision which someone had received, I don't accept any such list which makes the rounds, and I claim that all the lists drawn up before the 17th were fabricated, and fabricated by your client, Mr. Simo Zaric, because for a month prior to the events, such lists were all the talk on the radio, only creating hatred among the citizenry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the grounds of possessing a weapon, your husband was detained in the police station of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but people, Muslims and Croats, did not belong to a single national party. They did not possess weapons, and they were still detained. And it was that that we wondered about: Why were people being arrested and detained? Mr. Josip Bosolic [phoen] did not belong to any party, and he didn't have a weapon, and he paid with his life. A group of people was detained because of what they owned, because of the money that we had to pay to paramilitary units, and I can support that claim, because Mr. Bozo Stanisic had come to me and asked 5.000 Deutschmark as ransom, when five of my fellow citizens had died in the church, and he wanted this money as ransom for my brother-in-law's head.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that as far as members of the 4th Detachment were concerned, you saw them for the first time on the 18th of April, 1992, when they came to your house in the mission of collecting weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Boro. I saw uniformed people even before the 17th of April. You remember that rally we had for the togetherness of Yugoslavia, coexistence in Samac. Among other people, I saw the gentleman who worked in the Mebos company, nicknamed Sajkaca. Whether they belonged, he and the others, to the 4th Detachment or some other probably paramilitary formation or a JNA formation, I don't know. I saw the same kind of uniformed people at checkpoints when entering from Tuzla into Samac, at least on two occasions, and on one occasion, at Tisina, near the bridge, which means that I had no opportunity to see any lists, because the 4th Detachment had not been established publicly, naming the members and so on. The 4th Detachment was formed in a conspiracy, in secret. And you know this very well yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's put a time frame on it. We are now talking about the time period from the 17th of April, 1992, which means not prior to the 17th April, but only -- we are concerned with what happened after the 17th of April and in the time frame after that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 17th, and even not today, I still do not know all of the people who were members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have stated that you listened to Radio Samac broadcast, which from then on was something called Serbian Samac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and you were listening to the same broadcast, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Witness K, you are answering questions put to you by counsel in his capacity as counsel and as officer of the Court. You are not conversing with him. So please be -- avoid being rude to counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but since we are fellow citizens, I'm sure that I will not have this attitude when asked by a different counsel. But since this gentleman and I come from the same city, then my reaction is probably -- should not come as a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I'm not putting these questions to you because of myself; I'm putting these questions in order to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just get carried away, as if you and I were on an informal function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, can we agree that the then director and editor of the radio of Serbian Samac was Vaso Antic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that the journalists at the Serbian Samac radio were Ljubomir Cordasevic, Petar Andric, Radmilo Zigic, and some other girls that worked there as secretaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know the name of Ljubomir Cordasevic, I know Vaso Andric, but other than those two girls, I don't know if you have in mind Kosta's daughter, girl with the last name Lujic, then yes, I do know her. I did follow those broadcasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for me the fact that on the 17th and 18th of April, 1992, Serbian Samac radio read a declaration, a proclamation of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the proclamations were read, but whether those were proclamations of the Crisis Staff or some other institution, I don't know. It is probable that it was the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm the fact that these proclamations were mostly read by the director and the editor of the radio station, Mr. Vaso Antic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you in a position, are you able, to identify the individual who read out those proclamations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those proclamations were very often read out by Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, can I clarify the use of the constant phrase by you, or phrases by you, "can you confirm," "do you agree" or "can we agree." I'm not exactly clear what you mean whenever you say "can we agree," and "can you confirm." Are these your client's instructions, your own opinions, or what? I would have thought that if it's your client's instructions, then you put to her what his instructions are, and if you are unable to put anything on the basis of evidence which your client can give later, then you suggest to her. A suggestion is the natural corollary of certain events. So please use legal phraseology.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 20th of April, 1992, on Radio Samac, you heard a proclamation read out, proclamation by the commander of the 4th Detachment, of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Nikolic, the JNA detachment? I don't know a detachment of that kind. I know the 4th -- not the JNA, just the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know about the fact that the commander of the 4th Detachment of the JNA was Mr. Radovan Antic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I cannot accept this 4th Detachment being called as the 4th Detachment of the JNA. I know about the 4th Detachment, and I know that Mr. Antic was also a member of that 4th Detachment. I don't know what kind of a rank or a position he held in that detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: During those days, in April of 1992, there were frequently power outages in Bosanski Samac; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already stated so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm the fact that Serbian Samac radio did not have all-day broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the power would be there, and then it would go out, which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. means that whenever we had a power outage, we couldn't have a radio broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that in that period of time, on the Serbian Samac radio, a number of orders were broadcast concerning what the conduct of citizens should be in a situation of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. I've already stated so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And the call-up to enter names in the lists of Territorial Defence, which was issued by the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, its office in Samac, was something that was also broadcast over Serbian Samac radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and my husband responded to that call.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The invitation to attend a meeting at the Buducnost company, which was issued by the municipal staff of the TO, of the Serbian municipality Samac, was also something broadcast over Radio Samac; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this is why a lot of residents attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: Have you watched a special programme of the Novi Sad television concerning the situation in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly have. We had a power outage once, and this programme was re-broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You probably remember that in addition to other participants in that programme --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, could they state the name of the programme so we know which particular programme they're referring to, the name of the television show, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm sure you've heard Mr. Weiner's requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The programme was announced as a special programme. The title of the programme was "Events in Bosanski Samac." I'm not sure whether that was the working title of that programme, the exact working title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I should repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. You will agree that in that programme of the Novi Sad radio television, in addition to other participants, Mr. Simo Zaric also participated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on that occasion, Mr. Zaric discussed the situation in Bosanski Samac, illegal arming and mobilisation plans of the SDS and HDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He discussed those two plans, but not the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After that, have you had an occasion to see Simo Zaric participate in any kind of TV programme?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing him personally, but I did hear his voice on the Novi Sad television when religious buildings were blown up in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I could ask the witness a question, Mr. Pisarevic. I'm just wondering, Witness, how you could -- if you could explain how you didn't see him personally on the television but you heard his voice on the Novi Sad television. If you could just clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not sure whether it was a programme or it was just the news, and then perhaps during the news broadcast, they don't necessarily show a person; they simply show a report and then somebody is talking. So I'm not sure whether Mr. Zaric's person was shown on television, but I know for a fact that it was a report from Samac for the Novi Sad television, and we could hear the audio part but not see the visual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You will probably agree with me that Simo Zaric was not a journalist.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, you keep moving away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem with the transcript. I was just told that when I asked you whether you agreed that Mr. Simo Zaric was not a journalist, you responded "no." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Simo Zaric was not a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When testifying here before the Court Chamber, you said that you frequently heard Mr. Zaric talk on Radio Serbian Samac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, these frequent appearances of his on Radio Samac, did they take place after the 30th of April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to Mr. -- I heard Mr. Simo Zaric after the 30th of April as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that in Odzak municipality, there was a military administration which was introduced by the Krajina Corps of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just know that there were soldiers from Krajina there. Now, who was the entity that established the administration, I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that Simo Zaric was a member of the military political council in Odzak, in charge of security affairs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that he had an important function, but which function exactly it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You will probably agree with me that Mirko Pavic was a commander of police in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was also a command in Odzak, a command which belonged to the 1st Krajina Corps of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already replied that I did not know whether those were commands or whatever. I simply heard and saw that those were soldiers from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned checkpoints at the entry point in Odzak. Were those checkpoints manned by the members of the 1st Krajina Corps of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not know those soldiers. I don't know whether they were soldiers from Odzak or from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned in your testimony that Simo Zaric's sister, Jelena, with her underage son, was accommodated in the hotel in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and her underage son was not older than 16, but he was wearing a uniform and equipped with a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that Jelena Zaric, before the conflict broke out, lived and worked in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: In conversation with her, because Amira Tihic and I worked together, and Amira Tihic is friends with her, I know that she, herself, said that Muslims had helped her get out, and she probably mentioned where she had lived and worked, but I didn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Simo's sister, Koviljka she is married to Mujaga Omeranovic, a Muslim from Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of fact that Simo's sister, Simo's young sister, Nada, who is a doctor, is married to a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that Mr. Simo Zaric's wife, Fatima, is a Muslim by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know she was a Muslim, and I haven't really checked whether she is still one or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that Simo Zaric has a daughter by the name of Natasa and a son named Milan?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Son named "Mirel."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Natasa was in the same class as my daughter and Mirel now has a cafe in Samac, which my daughter frequents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You probably know that Simo Zaric brought up a stepson by the name of Denis, whose father is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. He brought up Fatima's child, but I don't know who his father is. I know only rumours, but nothing firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Simo's daughter Natasa married a Croat from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly do [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you asked Mr. Simo Zaric to help you and your kuma, [redacted] [redacted], you said that Simo Zaric told you on that occasion that you need to convert.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you exactly what I said. I first asked Mr. Simo Zaric whether he knew that my kuma, [redacted], was detained in Zasavica, to which he replied he didn't know that. And then I told him, "Now you know." Since Mr. Simo Zaric used to be this woman's boss, the director of her company, and they were good friends while she was living in Samac, I had good reason to address, to approach Mr. Simo Zaric to ask help in getting out of Samac. This is what he told me: "There are two ways for her to get out of Samac. One is to convert." And Simo Zaric wasn't cheating me. He wasn't deceiving me, because that was really one way of getting out of Samac. And the other way, he said, was to wait for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We will go into that in more detail. You will agree with the fact that no one who did not have a Serbian name and surname was able to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of everything. Perhaps somebody managed to get out. But to the extent that I talked to my fellow citizens, anyone who crossed over to Serbia or Hungary was forced to pay for documents in the name of a Serbian person, with a Serbian name and surname, and such papers were paid from 1.500 Deutschmark and higher. And then -- sorry. From 500 to 1.500 Deutschmark. And then people started to have less money. And these documents were provided by --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You know that many Croats and Muslims with false identity papers left for Serbia, that is, Yugoslavia, and further?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that they made their exit with identity papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Sorry. Counsel, before you go to the next question, the answer is -- you heard the answer she said. She made the exit with identity papers. Not what you put to her, that they got false ... Where is your question? Yes. Just the answer which she gave, yes. The implication is that they were not false identity papers, because her answer simply says they got -- they made their exit with identity papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that those identity papers with Serbian names and surnames on them were forged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know whether they were forged and how they allowed anyone to pass if they were, how they were accepted, but they were not issued in names like Tihic Amira. It was always something like Radojica, and then some Serbian last name. And how come one-third of the population of Samac was able to get out with that kind of documents if you claim that they were forged? And in order to get -- to procure such a document, the person not only had to change their name, but also had to pay the costs, and those costs were not within the limits of administrative stamp duties, 5, 10 Deutschmark. Those were larger amounts. The lowest amount was 500, and it varied up to 1.500 Deutschmark. And I suppose it was the authorities who should have established whether they were forged or not, these papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, can we reach an understanding finally? That is, let us clarify. If a document such as an identity card contains false, inaccurate personal details, then such a document is false, a forgery of some kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that I'm perfectly well aware of what is a forgery and what is not. I never had in my hands what you like to call a forgery. A forgery, to my mind, in such a situation, could have passed in one or two occasions. However, in our case, about one-third of the Muslim population got out with such papers. How come that the authorities which were in power at that time in Samac were unable to discover, to reveal and expose them as a forgery?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree that it was a false document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that a change of the first and last names does not mean necessarily that a person has changed their ethnic or religious affiliation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my mind, that's a very difficult thing to say, because I'm not the kind of person who was willing to change either my first or the last names, and I cannot speak on behalf of such people. But it is very well known to me that the citizens who had changed their names now have difficulty in changing them back. Those people had probably wanted to spare themselves the suffering that I went through. However, for some people, dignity is -- the sense of dignity is stronger than life itself. I am what I was born. I didn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You, as a person who studied law, are certainly aware that one could change one's name in administrative proceedings upon one's own request.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that conversion into Christianity and baptism is a religious rite conducted in church?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, where are these questions taking us, this exploration? Where is it taking us to? Please get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the first time before this Court, this witness mentioned conversion into Christianity and baptism. Since we believe that this is a very important issue, I want to discuss with the witness the method and procedure for such conversion into a different religion, and the difference that exists between a name change and conversion, plus whether a name change was made conditional upon conversion into a different religion, and to what extent conversion into a different religion affects one's affiliation to an ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: But where will this take you? Because basically, as I understand the witness, or as I understand what's happening, is that there are two ways to get out. One is you convert, and then you go to a proper authority and you have a Serb name. The other is not to convert, and to give a false Serbian name and somehow get the papers and leave, whether it's through officialdom, through corruption, or through other means. So where would that take you anyway, insofar as the issues of this case are concerned? I think perhaps you wish to concentrate on her particular evidence relating to herself, because this general discourse, many of the answers may just be speculative. So please go on with her evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that a name change, that is, a change of the first and last names, did not require necessarily to change one's religion and ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean during the war or before the war? No, no, no. I know that some people even went to church. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]. She is even the laughing stock now of some friends of mine of Serbian nationality, and I'm sorry to hear such jokes, because I think that's something that a person is entitled to, like changing a party. She was born to a Croat and a Muslim, that is, in a mixed marriage. She has -- she had a Muslim husband --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: She has a Croat husband. Correction.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: And she started going now to the Orthodox Church, because during the war that was impossible. The other two churches have not been restored, to this day, in Samac, after they were destroyed during the war. We could keep the Trial Chamber busy for an entire day listening to more examples. I know that these were forced conversions. People were forced to do that to spare themselves the suffering that perhaps 90 per cent of citizens had to go through, and 10 per cent were spared. And these people, after converting, were allowed perhaps to stay at home and not go to forced labour. But who exactly in Samac did this, I cannot put my finger on it to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think now is the time for a break, or shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will have a break and continue at 11.30 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, may I just very briefly raise one issue? It's nothing to do with this witness or the proceedings. That's this: Your anticipated schedule for your hearing of submissions or any further submissions on the admission of the variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understood from comments made by the Chamber just recently that you intended to deal with the matter at some point in the changing of witnesses and so on. May I respectfully ask that if you do want to do -- deal with that issue at such a point, could we do so at the conclusion of the next witness' evidence, following the next witness' evidence, because there are some matters that I want to attend to? If that causes any inconvenience to the Chamber, then I would prefer to deal with it not before then, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. You are asking the Chamber to deal with that after the next witness is through.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not asking the Chamber to deal with it at any specific time, but I ask not before the conclusion of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Whenever the Chamber wants, but thereafter, if it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination is continuing with Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of July, 1992, you were told for the first time that you had to go to work in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the first day you went to work in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it to be the 18th of July. I'm not sure, but it was immediately after Kornica. I went to Kornica for two or three days, perhaps five. I don't know myself any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In front of the local commune building in Bosanski Samac, you were told by the clerk for work obligation that you were to go to work in Odzak that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every morning I would be told by the clerk, who would read out from a list a group of people who were to go to Odzak, to Kornica, to work. This is how we knew where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And each time one armed individual would accompany you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be a driver and one armed individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you would come to Odzak, you would normally stop before the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The individual escorting you would give you work tasks for that day; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would normally be given orders from the gentleman who would be there, whether it would be Mirko Pavic or somebody else, and the others would be given tasks by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have stated before this Chamber that you went to Odzak until the 11th of August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and then I stopped because I had to take care of my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me: During those 20-something days from your first day until the 11th of August, how many times in total did you go to work in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that I didn't go some maybe two or three days either because my name was not called out or because I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How many times did Mirko Pavic help you by sending you to work in the MUP building in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever he was present when the group was brought in. Sometimes he simply wouldn't be present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that Mirko Pavic helped me at least three or four times. I'm not sure exactly. He certainly helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You stated before this Tribunal, and this is recorded in transcript page 4683, line 22, 23, that your husband was arrested on the orders of Stevan Todorovic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just a minute. There was no written order. There were three armed soldiers who came.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that your husband was arrested on the orders of Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of those three armed soldiers there was a boy, I think from Skarici, a young man from Skarici, who used to work at the department store, and he told me that pursuant to the orders of Mr. Todorovic, they had to arrest Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And Stevan Todorovic at the time was the chief of SUP; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, these three men who took your husband away, they took him to the SUP building, to the police building, where he was held; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And during the entire time, your husband was detained in the police station in Bosanski Samac; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 27th of November, he was taken to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. That's what you mean. Which means that your husband was kept in the police station in Bosanski Samac until the 27th of November of 1992; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what kind of uniforms those three men that arrested your husband were wearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had uniforms. I cannot remember what colour they were because I really -- those uniforms had no significance for me at the time. What was important for me was that my husband was being taken away. Now, whether somebody was blond or had dark hair or had blue or green uniform, this is simply something I did not pay attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony, you mentioned Slobodan, who used to work at the department store, at the wall-to-wall carpet section. Can we agree that he was a member of the police force in Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he weren't a member of police, he probably wouldn't have come to get my husband, and I cannot know this for certain. I cannot claim something. Because he didn't show me an arrest warrant, nor did he show me his police ID, which would indicate that he was a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Together with Jelena Kapetanovic and Ruza Matic, police took you to Zasavica; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were one or two men in the truck, and several of the policemen entered my house, because I -- some of them I knew, because they were policemen from prior to the war, and two young men I had never seen before in my municipality. The only person I recognised was Naser Sejdinovic, known as Cakar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that Naser Sejdic, known as Cakar, was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's probably Sejdic not Sejdinovic, as I've said. You are right. His last name is Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, is he a policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did other people who came to Zasavica, did they also come escorted by police there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, because when -- it certainly was the case when I was brought there, and I don't know about others, because it's something I didn't see. Now, when other people after me were brought in, I would generally meet them after they disembarked from the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I will put my last question to you, and I would ask that you reply by "yes" or "no" to it. Madam K, after Mr. Zaric surrendered to The Hague Tribunal in 1998, on the 24th of February, you have called his wife Fatima several times on the telephone; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why would I call her pursuant to somebody else talking me into that? Fatima and I have always had a good relationship. We never had any kind of conflict between us. We even meet to this day. Now, who should be the person to talk me into that, to put me up to call her, to put me up to call my former and present friend? I have no complaints as far as she is concerned. I have no problems talking to her. She was in Belgrade during the war, but we would normally talk regularly. So how is it -- Mrs. Fatima never asked me not to testify, although she did know that I was going to testify in the case of her husband.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, your reply means that you did call Fatima on telephone on a few occasions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps two or three times, perhaps even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The next counsel to cross-examine. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am. My name is Slobodan Zecevic. I am an attorney and I will put several questions to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be pleased to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will try, to the best of my ability, to avoid putting to you questions that could possibly identify you and members of your family, but I will kindly ask you to keep your mind on it and try not to say your name, your last name, to us. And the last thing I would ask you, if at all possible, could you please give very brief answers? Wait for my questions, and then give very brief answers. I will try to put to you questions which can be answered by "yes," "no," or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you will try and put clear and concise questions; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will do my best as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If your cross-examination requires private session, please say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Gentlemen, Your Honours. The first part of my cross-examination, in my opinion, does not require private session, and I will inform this Honourable Trial Chamber when I think it's needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you confirmed that you were not a member of the SDA several times during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your husband was a member of the SDA, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was one of the prominent members, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Based on your testimony here before this Tribunal concerning the night of the 16th and 17th, you said that he sat with Mr. Izetbegovic and Sulejman Tihic in Rustika, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He went to Rustika because I was worried that something was going on, and to see what was going on, and he stayed very briefly there and then came back home and then left again, and then shortly thereafter returned again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your husband attended meetings of the SDA, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband attended meetings very rarely. In the beginning, when the SDA was just established, he did attend them, but he was probably influenced by me in that decision. He was not a member of any of the committees, executive committees or I don't know what other committees existed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: While he attended those meetings, he probably told you what was going on at the SDA, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you were husband and wife.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't, because I was against national parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he -- did you perhaps in some other way find out that the SDA established an armed unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your husband did have an automatic rifle, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He got it from the TO, headed by late Milos Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, you are probably aware of the fact that your husband was the commander of one of the sections of that unit in charge of arming.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because in order to do that, he would have to sign some kind of a decision allocating him to that function. If my husband -- perhaps if he was a quartermaster, perhaps I would have believed that, but my husband is known to me, and everybody else from our town sitting here, as a person who can only go buy sugar and papers and do nothing else, and you know what qualities a quartermaster's post requires.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May the usher please show the witness document D24/2 ter, and I provided a folder number 1, and this is an official translation of the document which I received only a couple of days ago, Your Honours. And if the official translation can be put on the ELMO, one copy. The original before the witness, and the copy -- the English copies you can distribute, and one copy on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we just have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I was just reminded because there is a name, we should go into the private -- we should go into private, because it was under seal admitted. It was a sealed document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we should go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we should go into the closed session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Sorry. Just to clarify. [redacted] [redacted]; it belonged to Cadaster municipality. What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Cadaster municipality is actually the land registry. She is referring to the land registry of Samac, [redacted] [redacted], [redacted]. I can clarify that with the witness, if you like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Singh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Sorry. If the land was leased out from the municipality or whether they had bought it, [redacted] [redacted]-- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will pose that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, please tell me about [redacted], the land. The land and the house and everything on it, [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That land was entered in the land register of the Samac municipality. That's what you meant when you gave me your previous answer; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, could you please tell me: Your husband went to get that travel pass and got it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He got it in his own name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked one for me too, but they told him I didn't need one and I would be able to visit anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please just answer me: He got a pass in his name; is that correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your husband tell you on that occasion that he spent some time waiting in line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were other people waiting there. I don't know who they were. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So your husband told you that the people that he waited in line with were of Serbian ethnicity; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether they were of Serbian ethnicity or they were coming from a mixed background.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you that in addition to Milan Simic, he saw somebody else in the office, if you remember, madam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Jovanovic, or Ivanovic. It was a person who worked in the executive board of the Municipal Assembly. I think so. I don't know. I know this person by sight. At any case, it was somebody else sitting there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was it perhaps Mirko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know the name. This person came to Samac some year or two before the war. He was not originally from our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But he was the chairman of the executive board of the municipality at that time in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know whether he was a chairman of the executive board. I simply know that he worked in the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So let us sum up. This gentleman, Mr. Jovanovic, as far as you know, worked in the executive board of the Samac municipality in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he worked in the executive board. He did work -- he did have a job in the Municipal Assembly building. What exactly was his title, I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You just told us that your husband said that you didn't need a travel pass; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that he needed a pass because he was a person with a military duty and you were not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, you completed several years of law school, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So to some extent, you are familiar with regulations, laws, of the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the former regulations. And as far as the current ones are concerned, I am trying to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I had in mind were the regulations which were in force in April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, in that case, you probably know that military duty was an obligation for all men aged between 16 and 60; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In case of war or threat of war, a mobilisation of all military-aged men was proclaimed; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. There is some clarification in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will pose the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript reflected 16 and 60, whereas we said 18 and 60, isn't that so? The men aged between 18 and 60 had a military duty; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also know that in case of war and threat of war, all citizens had a work duty, including women; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: In former Yugoslavia, women also had their wartime assignments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, when you are assigned - perhaps you can help us with this - when there's mobilisation, as in this case you're saying there was, what happens? Do they send you a notice of mobilisation or they just come and take you away from your house?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you want me to explain that or should I ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you heard Judge Singh's question. When there was mobilisation, did they send call-ups or was there a general proclamation of mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no call-ups. The residents could hear, if they had a radio or any other source of information and were listening to it at that time, and at that time most of us were indeed listening. Then we would hear what was going on, on the radio. And the former law of the former Yugoslavia set forth that there would be couriers bringing in military call-up papers, indicating where each individual would go for their wartime assignments. And it was -- prior to that, all of the individuals with military duty had their wartime assignments, which could be changed once the war broke out, but not in the way it was done where we live.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, you and I are very familiar with this issue, but in order to explain this properly to the Trial Chamber, let us start from the beginning. Military duty, as you said, applied to all men aged between 18 and 60; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So all men who were part of military reserve had their wartime assignment well in advance to any kind of war or a threat of war; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This wartime assignment was entered into their military books, cards; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there was a decision to support it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but when that wartime assignment was entered into their military books or cards, they were considered official assignments, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This information would be entered into the military book based on the decision on wartime assignment received prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly so. So these decisions and their entering into the military books were performed by the national defence authorities; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was performed by them and also by the important work organisations, could do that as well, and this was further confirmed by the Territorial Defence or national defence authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you know, did your husband have a wartime assignment [redacted] [redacted] where he used to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, as far as you know, that in case of war, he had an obligation, just like everybody else, to go to his wartime assignment location? Is that how you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If he had a way of getting to his wartime assignment location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, absolutely. I don't mean just your husband; I mean everybody else. I asked you this question because I thought you know it would apply to everybody else. So that means that in case of war or threat of war, when a war or threat of war situation was proclaimed by relevant authorities, he would not be issued a separate call-up, but it was understood that he had an obligation to immediately go to his wartime assignment location; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if he had a way of getting there. My husband did not have a way of getting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I apologise for taking your husband as an example. My questions do not refer to your husband at all; I'm just asking a general question. What I'm saying pertained to everybody with a military obligation; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, including women, because women had such an obligation as well, in case they were able.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you properly, there was no special call-up for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mobilisation, but rather the residents were informed through mass media, by a proclamation issued through mass media; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe -- [Previous translation continues] ... or would you like me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just the last bit of my question. So he didn't end up [redacted] where he was supposed to go. He wasn't somewhere else. Perhaps you want to clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you have heard the question of the judge. So let me rephrase it. Your husband did not manage to get to his wartime assignment location; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband did not manage to get to [redacted] because that neighbourhood had already been taken by the paramilitary units, and three or four citizens had already been killed, and those were -- or perhaps they were wounded. And those were the people that tried to get to the veterinary station. And it includes Dr. Adnan Cizmic, who attempted to get through, and he was stopped somewhere between MUP and Agropromet company. He was shot in his leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You recently told us that your husband headed towards the TO building, [redacted].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband headed and then got to a certain place, and then he couldn't proceed because there was a lot of shooting going on. Now, whether my husband headed to [redacted] Territorial Defence building, this is something that you should have clarified with him, not with me. At any case, he wasn't able to get further from the bazaar. He came up to the house of his relative and then came back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So he spent only a brief time outside; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to the issue of work obligation. If I understood you correctly, you are familiar with the fact that in case of war or threat of war, there was a work obligation for all citizens; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, everybody who had a military obligation, men from 18 to 60 who were able, and women from 18 to 55, had a wartime assignment, including myself, which means that it included such jobs as dish washing, cooking, protecting archives, medical corps, quartermasters' duties, and a lot of other duties. You know, what else can be included? Everything that needs to be done during peacetime needs to be done during wartime. So women also had their wartime assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a bit of an objection. I just want a clarification. This is under the law of the former Yugoslavia. As the Prosecution has mentioned through witnesses, Bosnia-Herzegovina declared its independence. This concerns laws of the former Yugoslavia, and I would just request that when counsel asks these questions about these positions that one had to perform, this concerns the former government, not the government which was in place in April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel, you should clear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, we are now talking about the laws and regulations which were in force in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- please allow me to finish -- up until the 17th of April, 1992; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You and I were discussing laws of the former Yugoslavia. Please check the transcript. It should reflect it. Former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, former Yugoslavia was in existence on the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Bosnia had already been proclaimed at the time, and I really am not familiar with the laws of Bosnia, not even today's laws on national defence. I don't know whether they were adopted or not, and I did not look into these laws ever since Bosnia was proclaimed and up until the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think sometimes counsel does delve deeply into the status of the law then or at whatever time. I know that the witness did study law, but she is here as a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these questions which I was asking are really a common knowledge and have been -- they have been by all means known to everybody who lived in the former Yugoslavia. That is why I asked this witness. And more, because she happens to have a certain level of legal education. What I am trying now is to satisfy the request by this Honourable Trial Chamber made on the objection by my learned colleague. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- not getting into --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just have two questions. Please bear with me one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right, madam. So what you have said so far pertained to the rules in force in the territory of the former Yugoslavia at that time; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, madam: You mentioned your wartime assignment. Where was your wartime assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a wartime assignment in Bosnia, and as far as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is concerned, I did have one, and my wartime assignment was located in the work organisation of eight self-interest communities, but I was not bound by it any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understood you completely. You are now referring to the wartime assignment you had within the former Yugoslavia, and this was located in the building of self-interest communities where you used to work; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and once the new state was proclaimed, my previous wartime assignment was not valid any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your wartime assignment certainly didn't include you taking up a rifle and going and fighting; at least that was the concept in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since this is not a military secret any more, I can reveal my wartime assignment to you. My wartime assignment pertained to me working in my normal job in the self-interest community, dealing with welfare benefits, education issues, physical culture, culture, housing, and so on. So my wartime assignment did not at all include anything like taking up a broom and going to sweep.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So your official wartime assignment at this self-interest community included what you had just described, and that could also be referred to as the work obligation; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was called wartime assignment. In case of need, well, perhaps that could also be deemed to be work obligation, but let us not guess now. I actually do not know the answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in former Yugoslavia, all of the citizens had this civic duty and obligation; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everybody who was able and fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Including those men who were able and fit but did not go to their wartime units pursuant to their wartime assignment; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: You still have the former Yugoslavia in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: All conscripts in the former Yugoslavia had their wartime assignments, so if this conscript worked at a company called 11th April and his job entailed sweeping streets, then within that job, within that profession and those working skills, that person would get a similar wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. And similarly to that, your husband was given a wartime assignment [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, which was not valid on the 17th of April, my husband did not have to honour that wartime assignment on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, please have in mind what we're talking about. We are talking about the former Yugoslavia. This is what we're talking about. So my question was as follows: Was the same wartime assignment as the example you gave us for people working at the 11th April company, did it also apply to your husband? Your husband had a wartime assignment [redacted] [redacted], and during the war he would probably have tasks which were similar to his peacetime tasks and he would not be required to go and shoot with his rifle; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, if Yugoslavia had remained whole, if Bosnia and Herzegovina had not been proclaimed, he would never have been invited to the TO to take a rifle. So that means that his wartime assignment had probably become null and void, because Bosnia and Herzegovina was no longer part of Yugoslavia. So he got an invitation, or a summons, went to the TO and took that rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try once again, as clearly as I can, to put this question. Please answer it with a "yes," "no," or "I don't know," and please do your best, too. I'm trying to make this as short as possible, because we are talking about things that don't really matter to this particular examination.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I am still trying to answer with a "yes" or "no" whenever I can, but if a question is not as simple as that, then I want the Trial Chamber to understand what we are talking about, what is at issue. Because not all questions can be answered by yes or no. Some things simply remain unsaid, hanging in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. But please, do try. According to the regulations prevailing in the former Yugoslavia, this civic duty applied to all citizens, regardless of their ethnic background; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have spoken here about your husband and son, who commenced in their working obligation slightly before you did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They responded to the general mobilisation call-up.
